{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-hi-x","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"e1ac01ea9263a10fc93916f52897f140026164d929a51b6fed9661008648cda9","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-hi-class-3:lineage:101","source_registry_sha256":"1323c0f691f132d6e9e9a263c68306b972b82c8bbaa5a48a33a79177660764be","source_liveness_sha256":"27cf6d56fae2d5323c61bcbb69f0d992aeceb71a7dae4302b1f14baa17651cb0"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Driving Habits, Distracted and Defensive Driving, Trip Preparation and Safety Belts","heading":"C — Driving Habits, Distracted and Defensive Driving, Trip Preparation and Safety Belts","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Driving Habits, Distracted and Defensive Driving, Trip Preparation and Safety Belts

FACT_ID: sec12-F01 | anchor: A01
A habit forms when you do the same thing so many times that it becomes automatic, and driving habits form because the same physical actions are repeated over and over while your natural tendency to reduce those actions, without thinking, produces bad habits [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F02 | anchor: A01
Bad driving habits are caused by five things, laziness, impatience, inattention, arrogance and ignorance [A01].
Why it matters: the five causes are the chapter's organizing list.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F03 | anchor: A01
Laziness shows when the head-turn look behind for traffic before changing lanes, leaving the curb or opening a door on the traffic side shrinks to a mirror glance and then to an occasional check, and when the signal before such moves is dropped, a pair of habits that can cause a first crash [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F04 | anchor: A01
Impatience shows when pressure from following vehicles and an empty cross street tempt a driver to make only a good try at stopping at a stop sign or red light, even for a right turn, until the stop becomes a mere slowing down [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F05 | anchor: A01
The impatient driver speeds from stop to stop, weaves through traffic and tailgates when blocked, disrupting traffic and raising crash risk without realizing it [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F06 | anchor: A01
Inattention grows as a new driver who sat up straight with a firm grip and full awareness relaxes, leans back, loosens the grip and lets attention wander, and then the vehicle wanders too [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F07 | anchor: A01
The inattentive driver drives with one arm out the window [A01], gestures while talking to passengers, pays little attention to traffic, daydreams or gazes off the road when alone, and forfeits safety through that inattention [A02].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec12-F08 | anchor: A02
Where the impatient driver is merely in a hurry, the arrogant driver is purposely in a hurry, treats the vehicle as an extension of ego, ignores traffic laws and others' right of way, and should never be competed with or imitated, because there is nothing to gain and too much to lose [A02].
Why it matters: the arrogant versus impatient distinction is drawn explicitly in the text.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F09 | anchor: A02
The ignorant driver does not know sign meanings, markings, right-of-way rules or safe procedures, turns from the wrong lane, drives too slowly from uncertainty, stops at the end of a freeway on-ramp or crosses markings that prohibit crossing, and usually blames other drivers [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F10 | anchor: A02
A driver with a combination of bad habits who is in a crash is sure it just happened and was unavoidable, and further bad habits include failing to yield, skipping safety belts, drinking before the drive home, backing without checking that the area is clear, and being distracted by passengers, maps or lighting smoking materials [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F11 | anchor: A02
Good driving habits form just as easily as bad ones by deliberately repeating the proper action until it becomes automatic, making trips more enjoyable for you and more comfortable for passengers [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F12 | anchor: A02
Anything that takes your attention from driving can lead to a poor choice, so avoid eating, drinking, phoning, writing, reading, smoking, grooming, changing music, looking at things outside or inside the vehicle, talking to passengers, dealing with children or pets, applying makeup or shaving, and handle such things before you start or pull over safely first [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec12-F13 | anchor: A03
Keep the stereo low enough to hear sirens, horns and screeching tires outside the vehicle, and never drive with headsets or earphones covering or inserted in both ears, because they make emergency horns and sirens too hard to hear [A03].
Why it matters: the ban is on covering both ears, which is why it is tested.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F14 | anchor: A03
Talking on a cell phone pulls attention toward the conversation even with hands-free equipment, so avoid the phone or radio while moving, pull over in a safe place to make a call, and keep pets in a carrier rather than in the driver's lap [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F15 | anchor: A03
Defensive driving means identifying dangerous situations and acting against the danger before a crash situation develops, defending against aggressive, careless, inattentive, impulsive, ignorant and intoxicated drivers and pedestrians, and first defending against yourself if you show any of those traits [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F16 | anchor: A03
To avoid crashes a defensive driver stays alert with eyes moving, looks well ahead to anticipate chain-reaction situations, keeps an alternate plan and a way out, maintains proper following distance, and maintains proper speed for all highway conditions [A03].
Why it matters: the five defensive driving rules are a classic list question.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F17 | anchor: A03
Almost all the information needed to drive safely comes from looking and seeing, with constant awareness of conditions near the vehicle and special attention to conditions a considerable distance ahead, and speed reduces your field of vision [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec12-F18 | anchor: A04
Seeing should occupy your whole attention, using a scanning pattern that keeps most attention ahead with regular glances to the sides, the rear-view mirror and the instrument panel, because crash statements that begin with I did not see usually mean I was not paying attention [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec12-F19 | anchor: A04
Do not drive when ill, injured, emotionally upset or under the influence of intoxicants, follow your physician's advice when taking medication, get help from friends or public transportation for a necessary trip, and call the police in an emergency [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec12-F20 | anchor: A04
Correct any defect affecting safe operation as soon as possible, check or have checked the coolant, oil, battery water, tire condition and pressure and lamps if they have not been checked within the previous week, keep the windshield and windows clean, and make sure there is enough fuel to complete the trip [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec12-F21 | anchor: A04
In an unfamiliar vehicle, take a few minutes to locate and try the turn and hazard signals, head lamps and beam selector, wipers and washers, brakes, gear selector and horn, and fix any defect before driving [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec12-F22 | anchor: A04
When driving to an unfamiliar area know the exact destination and check it on a map first, choose the route with traffic, road, weather and light conditions in mind, allow enough time, and postpone or cancel the trip if you doubt you can cope comfortably with the conditions [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec12-F23 | anchor: A04
When the ignition is turned on every warning lamp on the instrument panel should light, a lamp that stays dark is not working, and after the computer check the warnings should go out, with a yellow light that stays on being a warning and a red light meaning danger to be checked immediately [A04].
Why it matters: yellow means warning, red means danger, and a dark lamp means a dead bulb.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec12-F24 | anchor: A05
Releasing the parking brake should turn the brake warning lamp off, and a lamp that comes on when the foot brake is pressed means the brake system is defective and the vehicle must not be driven [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec12-F25 | anchor: A05
Safety belts must be worn at all times when driving or riding, and they protect you by keeping you from being thrown from the car, from striking the windshield or interior, from injuring others by being thrown against them, and from being thrown out of the driver's seat where you control the vehicle [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec12-F26 | anchor: A05
Being thrown from the car makes death five times more likely, lap and shoulder belts make a crash survivable at speeds up to sixty miles per hour, and an unbelted occupant can be killed at speeds as low as twelve miles per hour [A05].
Why it matters: five times, sixty and twelve are the three numbers on this page.
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec12-F27 | anchor: A05
In a crash, infants and small children can be crushed to death by occupants who are not wearing seat belts, and the first impact often throws an unbelted driver away from the controls [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec12-F28 | anchor: A05
A lap belt should fit snugly across the hip bones and lower abdomen, the shoulder belt should be just loose enough to fit your fist between the belt and your chest, and belts in late-model vehicles allow body movement and lock only on impact [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec12-F29 | anchor: A05
Children too small for regular belts need special child seats, no person is strong enough to hold even a small infant in a crash or sudden stop, a child must never ride in someone's lap or stand on a seat, and the five seconds it takes to buckle up can save years of severe handicap [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec12-F30 | anchor: A06
When a car hits a barrier at thirty miles per hour it crushes and slows, but an unbelted person keeps moving forward inside the car at thirty miles per hour [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec12-F31 | anchor: A06
The car stops about one tenth of a second after impact, and about one fiftieth of a second later the unbelted person slams into the dashboard and windshield in the human collision, which takes only one hundredth of a second [A06].
Why it matters: the timeline contrasts the car's one-tenth-second stop with the person's one-hundredth-second stop.
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec12-F32 | anchor: A06
A belted occupant moves forward only until the belts restrain the body, keeping head and chest off the interior, and rides down the collision as part of the car's slower, energy-absorbing stop, so for belted people there is no human collision [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec12-F33 | anchor: A07
Wear the lap and shoulder belt low and snug, place a baby in a car safety seat using an infant seat or a convertible seat in the infant or toddler position, and never carry a baby in your arms [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec12-F34 | anchor: A07
A household carrier, travel bed or cloth carrier must not be used in place of a car safety seat, and clothing with legs lets the harness fit snugly while a papoose bunting or sack sleeper does not [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec12-F35 | anchor: A07
Common car seat mistakes are an infant facing forward, a harness not used or not snug, and a seat belt in the wrong place, not tight or not used, and in cold weather the baby is not wrapped in a blanket under the harness but has the straps pulled through holes cut in the blanket, which is folded over after buckling [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0063]

Misconceptions: hands-free equipment does not remove the distraction of a phone call; a single earphone is tolerated but covering both ears is not; a dark warning lamp at ignition means a dead bulb, not a healthy system; a yellow lamp that stays on is a warning while red means danger; the shoulder belt is worn slightly looser than the snug lap belt; an unbelted crash can kill at twelve miles per hour, and belts make crashes survivable up to sixty; an infant seat faces rearward, and facing an infant forward is a listed mistake.

Mnemonics: Lazy, impatient, inattentive, arrogant, ignorant are the five bad-habit causes; alert eyes, look ahead, keep a way out, keep your distance, keep your speed are the five defensive rules; five times deadlier thrown out, survivable to sixty belted, deadly at twelve unbelted.

Glossary: defensive driving (spotting hazards and acting before a crash situation develops); human collision (the occupant's impact with the car interior after the car itself has stopped); scanning pattern (eyes mostly ahead with regular glances to sides, mirror and panel); convertible seat (a child seat usable in infant and toddler positions); beam selector (the headlight high and low beam control).

Dynamic facts: none; habit, distraction, defensive driving and belt guidance are stable teaching content in this edition, and the belt statistics are stated only as printed.
